author: Gregory Thaumaturgus
occasion: The work defends orthodox Christology against positions that either deny the createdness of Christ's body or confuse his flesh with his divinity. Each chapter anathematizes a specific error and briefly argues against it.
argument: Gregory argues that Christ's body is created, not uncreated, because what is uncreated cannot suffer, be wounded, or be touched, yet the risen Christ showed the nails and the wound made by the lance, and his body able to be touched, to the disciples, entering through closed doors. He also argues that Christ's flesh is not consubstantial with the divinity, since consubstantiality means identity of nature and eternal existence, whereas the flesh exists in time. In both cases he affirms that Christ is truly God and truly man: when he was otherwise God, he was recognized as man; and when he was truly man, God was nevertheless demonstrated from his own works.

outline.move: Anathematizes those who call Christ's body uncreated, arguing that the uncreated cannot suffer or be touched, while the risen Christ showed the nails and the wound made by the lance, and his body able to be touched, to the disciples.
Anathematizes those who say Christ's flesh is consubstantial with the divinity, arguing that consubstantiality requires identity of nature and eternity, which flesh lacks.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The incarnate Word, true God and true man, whose body is created and whose divinity is eternal.

scripture: The author cites Philippians 2:6-7 (form of God, self-emptying, form of a servant) and alludes to resurrection appearances involving the nails, lance wound, body able to be touched, and entering through closed doors. The source does not specify which Gospel accounts are alluded to; the details combine elements from multiple resurrection accounts without explicit citation. Biblical citations should follow modern conventions: Philippians 2:6-7.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Christus autem a mortuis resurgens clavorum et vulnerationem lancea factam corpusque suum palpandum discipulis demonstrans clausis ianuis ingressus est.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source states Christ entered 'clausis ianuis' (with closed doors), but this is presented as a separate action from demonstrating his body to the disciples, not as part of the resurrection appearance to the disciples where he showed the nails and wound. The grammar suggests: rising from the dead, showing the nails, the wound made by lance, and his touchable body to the disciples, [and] entering through closed doors. The 'entering through closed doors' is not explicitly connected to the same event as the demonstration to the disciples.

_unresolved_facts.claim: when he was otherwise God, he was recognized as man; and when he was truly man, God was nevertheless demonstrated from his own works
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: et cum alioqui Deus esset, homo agnoscebatur; et cum esset vere homo, Deus tamen ex suis operibus ostendebatur
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source uses 'alioqui' (otherwise/nevertheless/in other respects) not 'when he was otherwise God.' The structure is: 'and although he was God in other respects, he was recognized as man; and when he was truly man, God was nevertheless demonstrated from his own works.' The brief's 'when he was otherwise God' misrepresents 'alioqui Deus esset' which indicates God's other/remaining divine status concurrent with incarnation, not a temporal 'when.'

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Christus autem a mortuis resurgens clavorum et vulnerationem lancea factam corpusque suum palpandum discipulis demonstrans clausis ianuis ingressus est.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline should not include 'entering through closed doors' as part of the demonstration to the disciples, as the Latin grammar presents this as a separate participial clause, not as part of what was demonstrated to the disciples.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: in forma Dei et Deum esse ante saecula, et seipsum exinanisse, et formam servi accepisse
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source cites 'in forma Dei...et Deum esse ante saecula, et seipsum exinanisse, et formam servi accepisse' which corresponds to Philippians 2:6-7, but the source also includes 'et Deum esse ante saecula' (and to be God before the ages), which is not in Philippians 2:6-7. This appears to be a conflation with other passages (possibly John 1:1 or similar). The citation should be noted as a loose or expanded rendering of Philippians 2:6-7 with additional theological content.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The source does not specify which Gospel accounts are alluded to; the details combine elements from multiple resurrection accounts without explicit citation.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source explicitly marks the incarnation material with 'sicut scriptum est' (as it is written) in section 1, and again in section 2 for the Philippians material. The brief correctly notes no explicit Gospel citation for the resurrection details, but should note that 'sicut scriptum est' does appear in section 1, though its referent is unclear—it may refer to the incarnation formula rather than the resurrection details specifically.
